paragraphs.heading: What a steroid is
paragraphs.text: A steroid is an organic compound built around four rings fused together, labelled A, B, C and D, in a set arrangement. Hundreds of them occur in fungi, plants and animals. Familiar examples include the lipid cholesterol, the sex hormones estradiol and testosterone, anabolic steroids, and dexamethasone, a corticosteroid drug that fights inflammation.

paragraphs.heading: Two jobs in living things
paragraphs.text: Steroids have two chief roles in biology. Some are built into cell membranes, where they change how fluid the membrane is. Others act as signaling molecules.

paragraphs.heading: The four-ring core
paragraphs.text: Every steroid and sterol shares one core, called gonane, which also has the long name cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene. It is usually made of seventeen carbon atoms joined into four fused rings with a three-dimensional shape. Rings A, B and C each have six members and are cyclohexane rings. Ring D has five members and is a cyclopentane ring.

paragraphs.heading: How steroids differ
paragraphs.text: Steroids vary in which chemical groups hang off this core and in how oxidized the rings are. Sterols are the steroids that carry a hydroxy group at position three, on a skeleton derived from cholestane. Cholesterol, for instance, has a hydroxyl group at C-3, while testosterone and progesterone carry a carbonyl group there. Some steroids are changed more drastically: cutting ring B gives secosteroids, and vitamin D₃ is one of them.

paragraphs.heading: Where steroids come from
paragraphs.text: Cells make every steroid from a sterol starting material. In the group of living things called opisthokonts, those are cholesterol and lanosterol; in plants it is cycloartenol. All three are made by closing the triterpene squalene into rings.

paragraphs.heading: How they get their names
paragraphs.text: The word steroid comes from cholesterol, a sterol first described in gall stones. Its name joins the Ancient Greek chole-, meaning bile, and stereos, meaning solid. Chemists name many steroids from parent structures such as pregnane and androstane, or from well-known natural ones such as progesterone, testosterone and cortisol. So 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is progesterone with an added hydroxy group at position 17, and 11-deoxycortisol is cortisol lacking the oxygen at position 11.

paragraphs.heading: Alpha and beta
paragraphs.text: Steroid chemists mark which way a group points with the Greek letters α and β. Broadly, α means a group is oriented toward the plane of the rings, and β means it is oriented away from it. In drawings, α bonds appear as dashed wedges and β bonds as solid wedges.
